name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Industrial catalysts and their chemical processes

questiontext.text:
Match the catalyst listed in List I with the corresponding industrial process or reaction in List II:

List I (Catalyst) List II (Process / Reaction)
(A) \(\text{V}_2\text{O}_5\) (I) Manufacture of ammonia
(B) Finely divided \(\text{Fe}\) (II) Oxidation of ethyne to ethanal (Wacker process)
(C) \(\text{PdCl}_2\) (III) Manufacture of sulphuric acid (Contact process)
(D) \(\text{TiCl}_4\) with \(\text{Al(CH}_3)_3\) (IV) Manufacture of polyethylene

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transition metals and their compounds exhibit notable catalytic activity due to their variable oxidation states, ability to form complexes, and provision of suitable reaction pathways by adsorption and bond weakening.

Step 2: Evaluation of individual catalytic applications
- Vanadium(V) oxide (\(\text{V}_2\text{O}_5\)) catalyses the oxidation of \(\text{SO}_2\) to \(\text{SO}_3\) in the Contact process during the manufacture of sulphuric acid.
- Finely divided iron (\(\text{Fe}\)) is used as the heterogeneous catalyst in the Haber process for the synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
- Palladium(II) chloride (\(\text{PdCl}_2\)) serves as the catalyst in the Wacker process for the oxidation of ethyne to ethanal.
- Titanium tetrachloride with trimethylaluminium (\(\text{TiCl}_4 + \text{Al(CH}_3)_3\)) forms the Ziegler–Natta catalyst utilized in the coordination polymerisation of ethene to manufacture polyethylene.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each catalyst with its process results in: \(\text{V}_2\text{O}_5\) with the manufacture of sulphuric acid (Contact process), finely divided \(\text{Fe}\) with the manufacture of ammonia, \(\text{PdCl}_2\) with the oxidation of ethyne to ethanal (Wacker process), and \(\text{TiCl}_4 + \text{Al(CH}_3)_3\) with the manufacture of polyethylene. Hence, the correct correspondence is (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Aqueous colors of first row transition ions

questiontext.text:
Match the hydrated transition metal ion in List I with its characteristic aqueous solution color in List II:

List I (Aqueous Ion) List II (Observed Color)
(A) \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) (I) Yellow
(B) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) (II) Purple
(C) \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) (III) Pink
(D) \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) (IV) Green

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The color of aquated transition metal ions arises from \(d\text{–}d\) electronic transitions wherein an electron from a lower energy \(d\) orbital absorbs visible light to promote to a higher energy \(d\) orbital. The complementary color of the absorbed radiation is transmitted and perceived.

Step 2: Identification of individual ion colors
- Titanium(III) ion (\(\text{Ti}^{3+}\), configuration \(3d^1\)) exhibits a characteristic purple color.
- Iron(III) ion (\(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), configuration \(3d^5\)) produces a yellow solution in aqueous medium.
- Nickel(II) ion (\(\text{Ni}^{2+}\), configuration \(3d^8\)) exhibits a distinctive green color.
- Manganese(II) ion (\(\text{Mn}^{2+}\), configuration \(3d^5\)) displays a characteristic pale pink color.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Correlating each ion to its color gives: \(\text{Ti}^{3+}\) matches purple, \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) matches yellow, \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) matches green, and \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) matches pink. This establishes the set (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Spin only magnetic moments of divalent ions

questiontext.text:
Match the divalent gaseous/aqueous transition metal ion in List I with its calculated spin-only magnetic moment in List II:

List I (Divalent Ion) List II (Magnetic Moment, \(\mu\) / BM)
(A) \(\text{V}^{2+}\) (I) \(4.90\text{ BM}\)
(B) \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) (II) \(2.84\text{ BM}\)
(C) \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) (III) \(3.87\text{ BM}\)
(D) \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) (IV) \(5.92\text{ BM}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Formula and Principle
The spin-only magnetic moment is calculated using the relation: \[\mu = \sqrt{n(n + 2)}\text{ BM}\] where \(n\) is the number of unpaired \(d\)-electrons.

Step 2: Electronic configuration and unpaired electron count
- Vanadium (\(Z = 23\)): Neutral atom is \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^3\,4s^2\). For \(\text{V}^{2+}\), the outer configuration is \(3d^3\). The number of unpaired electrons is \(n = 3\). \[\mu = \sqrt{3(3 + 2)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\text{ BM}\] - Manganese (\(Z = 25\)): Neutral atom is \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^2\). For \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\), the outer configuration is \(3d^5\). The number of unpaired electrons is \(n = 5\). \[\mu = \sqrt{5(5 + 2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{ BM}\] - Iron (\(Z = 26\)): Neutral atom is \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^6\,4s^2\). For \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\), the outer configuration is \(3d^6\). The number of unpaired electrons is \(n = 10 - 6 = 4\). \[\mu = \sqrt{4(4 + 2)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{ BM}\] - Nickel (\(Z = 28\)): Neutral atom is \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^8\,4s^2\). For \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\), the outer configuration is \(3d^8\). The number of unpaired electrons is \(n = 10 - 8 = 2\). \[\mu = \sqrt{2(2 + 2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.84\text{ BM}\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching the calculated values yields: \(\text{V}^{2+}\) corresponds to \(3.87\text{ BM}\), \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) corresponds to \(5.92\text{ BM}\), \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) corresponds to \(4.90\text{ BM}\), and \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) corresponds to \(2.84\text{ BM}\). Thus, the correct sequence is (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Highest oxides and oxocations oxidation states

questiontext.text:
Match the transition metal oxide or oxocation in List I with the oxidation state of the central transition metal in List II:

List I (Species) List II (Oxidation State)
(A) \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\) (I) \(+4\)
(B) \(\text{CrO}_3\) (II) \(+5\)
(C) \(\text{VO}_2^+\) (III) \(+6\)
(D) \(\text{TiO}^{2+}\) (IV) \(+7\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principles
The oxidation state of the transition metal is determined from the neutral molecule or net cationic charge by assigning each oxo ligand an oxidation state of \(-2\).

Step 2: Evaluation of individual species
- For \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\): Let the oxidation state of \(\text{Mn}\) be \(x\). \[2x + 7(-2) = 0 \implies 2x = 14 \implies x = +7\] - For \(\text{CrO}_3\): Let the oxidation state of \(\text{Cr}\) be \(x\). \[x + 3(-2) = 0 \implies x = +6\] - For dioxovanadium(V) cation \(\text{VO}_2^+\): Let the oxidation state of \(\text{V}\) be \(x\). \[x + 2(-2) = +1 \implies x - 4 = +1 \implies x = +5\] - For oxotitanium(IV) cation \(\text{TiO}^{2+}\): Let the oxidation state of \(\text{Ti}\) be \(x\). \[x + 1(-2) = +2 \implies x = +4\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each species to the deduced oxidation state yields: \(\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7\) corresponds to \(+7\), \(\text{CrO}_3\) corresponds to \(+6\), \(\text{VO}_2^+\) corresponds to \(+5\), and \(\text{TiO}^{2+}\) corresponds to \(+4\). This establishes the set (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Permanganate oxidations in neutral and acidic media

questiontext.text:
Match the reactant being oxidised by potassium permanganate (\(\text{KMnO}_4\)) in List I with the principal oxidized product formed in List II:

List I (Reactant and Medium) List II (Oxidized Product)
(A) \(\text{I}^-\) in neutral or faintly alkaline medium (I) \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\)
(B) \(\text{I}^-\) in acidic medium (II) \(\text{CO}_2\)
(C) \(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}\) in neutral or faintly alkaline medium (III) \(\text{IO}_3^-\)
(D) \(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\) in acidic medium at \(333\text{ K}\) (IV) \(\text{I}_2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical reactions of permanganate
Potassium permanganate acts as a strong oxidant whose reduction pathway and resulting oxidized products depend strictly on the pH of the medium.

Step 2: Evaluation of each specific transformation
- Oxidation of iodide in neutral/faintly alkaline medium: Iodide is quantitatively oxidized to iodate: \[2\text{MnO}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- + \text{IO}_3^-\] - Oxidation of iodide in acidic medium: Iodide is oxidized to elemental iodine: \[2\text{MnO}_4^- + 16\text{H}^+ + 10\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} + 5\text{I}_2\] - Oxidation of thiosulphate in neutral/faintly alkaline medium: Thiosulphate is oxidized almost quantitatively to sulphate: \[8\text{MnO}_4^- + 3\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 8\text{MnO}_2 + 6\text{SO}_4^{2-} + 2\text{OH}^-\] - Oxidation of oxalate in acidic medium at \(333\text{ K}\): Oxalate is oxidized to carbon dioxide: \[2\text{MnO}_4^- + 16\text{H}^+ + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} + 10\text{CO}_2\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each reactant and condition with its primary product yields: \(\text{I}^-\) in neutral medium gives \(\text{IO}_3^-\), \(\text{I}^-\) in acidic medium gives \(\text{I}_2\), \(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}\) in neutral medium gives \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\), and \(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}\) in acidic medium gives \(\text{CO}_2\). This corresponds to (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

questiontext.text:
Match the reagent reacting with a lanthanoid metal (\(\text{Ln}\)) in List I with the resulting chemical product in List II:

List I (Reagent / Condition) List II (Product Formula)
(A) Heated with Nitrogen (\(\text{N}_2\)) (I) \(\text{LnC}_2\)
(B) Heated with Sulphur (\(\text{S}\)) (II) \(\text{LnN}\)
(C) Heated with Carbon (\(\text{C}\)) at \(2773\text{ K}\) (III) \(\text{Ln(OH)}_3 + \text{H}_2\)
(D) Reaction with water (\(\text{H}_2\text{O}\)) (IV) \(\text{Ln}_2\text{S}_3\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Chemical behavior of lanthanoids
Lanthanoids generally form compounds in their most stable oxidation state of \(+3\). Their standard reactivity resembles highly electropositive metals like calcium or aluminium.

Step 2: Evaluation of products
- Heating with nitrogen gas: Lanthanoids react directly with nitrogen to form mononitrides of composition \(\text{LnN}\).
- Heating with sulphur: Lanthanoids react with sulphur to yield sesquisulphides of composition \(\text{Ln}_2\text{S}_3\).
- Heating with carbon at elevated temperatures (\(2773\text{ K}\)): Lanthanoids combine with carbon to form dicarbides having the formula \(\text{LnC}_2\) (along with other stoichiometric carbides like \(\text{Ln}_3\text{C}\) and \(\text{Ln}_2\text{C}_3\)).
- Reaction with water: Lanthanoids react with water to form basic trihydroxides with liberation of hydrogen gas, following the stoichiometry \(\text{Ln(OH)}_3 + \text{H}_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching the reagents to products yields: heating with nitrogen gives \(\text{LnN}\), heating with sulphur gives \(\text{Ln}_2\text{S}_3\), heating with carbon gives \(\text{LnC}_2\), and reaction with water gives \(\text{Ln(OH)}_3 + \text{H}_2\). This corresponds to (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Electronic configurations of f block tripositive ions

questiontext.text:
Match the tripositive lanthanoid or actinoid ion in List I with its ground-state valence electronic configuration in List II:

List I (Tripositive Ion) List II (Valence Configuration)
(A) \(\text{Ce}^{3+}\) (\(Z = 58\)) (I) \(4f^7\)
(B) \(\text{Gd}^{3+}\) (\(Z = 64\)) (II) \(5f^7\)
(C) \(\text{Lu}^{3+}\) (\(Z = 71\)) (III) \(4f^1\)
(D) \(\text{Cm}^{3+}\) (\(Z = 96\)) (IV) \(4f^{14}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principles of electronic configurations of \(f\)-block ions
In the formation of tripositive lanthanoid (\(\text{Ln}^{3+}\)) and actinoid (\(\text{An}^{3+}\)) ions, the outermost \(s\) electrons and any outer \(d\) electrons are removed first, leaving an \(f^n\) configuration.

Step 2: Configuration deduction
- Cerium (\(Z = 58\)): Ground-state neutral atom is \([\text{Xe}]\,4f^1\,5d^1\,6s^2\). Loss of three electrons (two from \(6s\) and one from \(5d\)) yields \(\text{Ce}^{3+}\) with the configuration \(4f^1\).
- Gadolinium (\(Z = 64\)): Ground-state neutral atom is \([\text{Xe}]\,4f^7\,5d^1\,6s^2\). Removal of three electrons leaves the half-filled stable core \([\text{Xe}]\,4f^7\).
- Lutetium (\(Z = 71\)): Ground-state neutral atom is \([\text{Xe}]\,4f^{14}\,5d^1\,6s^2\). Removal of three electrons leaves the completely filled stable core \([\text{Xe}]\,4f^{14}\).
- Curium (\(Z = 96\)): Ground-state neutral atom is \([\text{Rn}]\,5f^7\,6d^1\,7s^2\). Removal of three electrons gives \(\text{Cm}^{3+}\) with the half-filled configuration \(5f^7\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each ion with its electronic configuration results in: \(\text{Ce}^{3+}\) pairs with \(4f^1\), \(\text{Gd}^{3+}\) pairs with \(4f^7\), \(\text{Lu}^{3+}\) pairs with \(4f^{14}\), and \(\text{Cm}^{3+}\) pairs with \(5f^7\). This corresponds to (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Standard electrode potentials of transition couples

questiontext.text:
Match the redox couple of the first row transition metals in List I with its corresponding standard electrode potential value (\(E^\circ\)) in List II:

List I (Redox Couple) List II (\(E^\circ / \text{V}\))
(A) \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\) (I) \(+1.57\text{ V}\)
(B) \(\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+}\) (II) \(-0.41\text{ V}\)
(C) \(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+}\) (III) \(+0.77\text{ V}\)
(D) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}\) (IV) \(+0.34\text{ V}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Basis of Electrode Potentials
Standard reduction potentials reflect the combined energetic terms of atomisation, successive ionisations, and ionic hydration. For \(M^{3+}/M^{2+}\), the potential depends primarily on the magnitude of the third ionisation enthalpy and the electronic stability of the resulting configurations.

Step 2: Evaluation of individual potential values
- \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\): Copper has a positive \(E^\circ\) of \(+0.34\text{ V}\) because the sum of its high enthalpy of atomisation and high ionisation enthalpies is not compensated by the hydration enthalpy of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\).
- \(\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+}\): Possesses an unusually high positive potential of \(+1.57\text{ V}\) because reduction converts the less stable \(d^4\) ion into the exceptionally stable half-filled \(d^5\) ion (\(\text{Mn}^{2+}\)), accompanied by a very high third ionisation enthalpy of manganese.
- \(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+}\): Has a negative potential of \(-0.41\text{ V}\) because \(\text{Cr}^{2+}\) (\(d^4\)) readily undergoes oxidation to \(\text{Cr}^{3+}\) which possesses a stable, half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) sub-level.
- \(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}\): Shows a moderately positive potential of \(+0.77\text{ V}\), where \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) (\(d^5\)) has extra stability relative to \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) (\(d^6\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each redox couple with its value gives: \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\) matches \(+0.34\text{ V}\), \(\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+}\) matches \(+1.57\text{ V}\), \(\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+}\) matches \(-0.41\text{ V}\), and \(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}\) matches \(+0.77\text{ V}\). This corresponds to (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Structural and magnetic features of oxoanions

questiontext.text:
Match the oxoanion of transition metals in List I with its structural or magnetic characteristic in List II:

List I (Oxoanion) List II (Characteristic Feature)
(A) \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\) (I) Tetrahedral geometry, green color, paramagnetic (\(1\) unpaired electron)
(B) \(\text{MnO}_4^{2-}\) (II) Tetrahedral geometry, intense purple color, diamagnetic
(C) \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) (III) Two tetrahedra sharing a corner with a bond angle of \(126^\circ\)
(D) \(\text{CrO}_4^{2-}\) (IV) Discrete tetrahedral geometry, yellow color, converts to dichromate in acid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural and Electronic Principles
Chromate, dichromate, manganate, and permanganate are oxoanions where \(\pi\)-bonding arises from the overlap of \(p\)-orbitals of oxygen with \(d\)-orbitals of the transition metal.

Step 2: Analysis of individual oxoanions
- Dichromate ion (\(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\)): Consists of two tetrahedral units sharing a single oxygen corner, featuring bridging \(\text{Cr–O–Cr}\) bonds with an angle of \(126^\circ\).
- Manganate ion (\(\text{MnO}_4^{2-}\)): Possesses tetrahedral geometry with manganese in the \(+6\) oxidation state (\(3d^1\)). Because of the presence of one unpaired electron, it is paramagnetic and green in color.
- Permanganate ion (\(\text{MnO}_4^-\)): Possesses tetrahedral geometry with manganese in the \(+7\) oxidation state (\(3d^0\)). It lacks unpaired \(d\) electrons, making it diamagnetic, while exhibiting an intense purple color due to charge transfer.
- Chromate ion (\(\text{CrO}_4^{2-}\)): A discrete yellow tetrahedral species with chromium in the \(+6\) oxidation state; upon acidification, it undergoes condensation to form the orange dichromate ion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching the oxoanions to their features yields: \(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}\) matches two tetrahedra sharing one corner with a \(126^\circ\) angle, \(\text{MnO}_4^{2-}\) matches green and paramagnetic, \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) matches purple and diamagnetic, and \(\text{CrO}_4^{2-}\) matches discrete yellow tetrahedron converting to dichromate in acid. This corresponds to (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THE_D_AND_F_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Chemical rationale for transition element anomalies

questiontext.text:
Match the observed property/phenomenon of \(d\)- and \(f\)-block elements in List I with its primary underlying chemical cause in List II:

List I (Observed Phenomenon) List II (Primary Chemical Cause)
(A) Nearly identical atomic radii of \(\text{Zr}\) (\(160\text{ pm}\)) and \(\text{Hf}\) (\(159\text{ pm}\)) (I) Much more negative hydration enthalpy of the divalent ion overcompensating the second ionisation enthalpy
(B) Greater stability of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\) relative to \(\text{Cu}^+\text{(aq)}\) (II) Intervention and poor shielding of completely filled \(4f\) subshell across the lanthanoids
(C) Abnormally low enthalpy of atomisation of Zinc (\(126\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) (III) Less penetration of \(5f\) orbitals and poorer shielding by \(5f\) electrons compared to \(4f\)
(D) Greater extent of actinoid contraction compared to lanthanoid contraction (IV) Absence of unpaired \(d\)-electrons resulting in no contribution of \(d\)-electrons to metallic bonding

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Underlying Principles
Specific chemical and physical trends across the \(d\)- and \(f\)-block elements are governed by shielding capabilities of diffuse inner subshells, exchange stabilization, and thermodynamic enthalpy balances.

Step 2: Evaluation of each correlation
- The similarity in atomic radii between \(\text{Zr}\) and \(\text{Hf}\) is a direct consequence of the lanthanoid contraction, which is caused by the poor shielding effect of the fourteen \(4f\) electrons filled prior to the \(5d\) series, compensating for the expected normal increase in atomic size with increasing atomic number.
- The higher stability and disproportionation of copper(I) into copper(II) in aqueous solution occurs because the enthalpy of hydration for \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)}\) is much more negative than that for \(\text{Cu}^+\text{(aq)}\), which more than compensates for the energy required for the second ionisation of copper.
- Zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation (\(126\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) in the \(3d\) series because all its \(3d\) orbitals are completely filled (\(3d^{10}\)); hence, no unpaired \(d\) electrons participate in interatomic metallic bonding, leaving only weak metallic interactions involving \(4s\) electrons.
- Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction because \(5f\) orbitals penetrate less into the inner core, and \(5f\) electrons provide poorer shielding against the increasing nuclear charge than \(4f\) electrons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each phenomenon to its scientific cause gives: \(\text{Zr}/\text{Hf}\) radius similarity pairs with poor shielding of \(4f\) subshell (lanthanoid contraction), stability of aqueous \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) pairs with the highly negative hydration enthalpy overcoming the second ionisation enthalpy, low atomisation enthalpy of zinc pairs with absence of unpaired \(d\) electrons in metallic bonding, and greater actinoid contraction pairs with poorer shielding of \(5f\) compared to \(4f\). This corresponds to (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III).
